mainEntity.name: Which surfaces should be cleaned more often than everything else?

acceptedAnswer.text: The ones closest to the patient and touched most: plinth rails and adjustment levers, parallel bars, treadmill handrails and consoles, cable grips, dumbbell handles, door hardware, and treatment room light switches. CDC Core Practices 5b and Section II item A of the Infection Prevention Checklist call for high-touch surfaces near the patient to sit on a more frequent schedule than general environmental surfaces. In practice that means a mid-day high-touch circuit through the gym on top of the terminal clean, and that mid-day circuit is where most clinics have a gap.

mainEntity.name: Nobody here checks whether cleaning was done properly. Should we be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and the absence of checking is itself a finding. Section I item D of the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist expects evidence that the clinic monitors and assesses whether cleaning is consistently and correctly performed. We build that in: dated service logs by zone, a supervisor audit on a defined interval using a written checklist tied to your own protocol, and a corrective-action note whenever something misses. You keep the record. The point is not to grade our crew for you, it is that you can show an assessor a monitoring process that exists on paper.

mainEntity.name: What documentation do I get for a CARF survey or a DPH review?

acceptedAnswer.text: The written cleaning and disinfection policy covering the gym, treatment tables, and shared equipment, with responsibility assigned line by line; the equipment inventory flagging items with no manufacturer reprocessing instructions; the product list with EPA registration numbers and label contact times; SDS sheets; per-person training and competency records; dated service logs; and supervisor audit results. That set answers Section I items A through D of the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist directly. Dory's carries $2 million in general liability and will name your clinic on the certificate.

How we clean rehabilitation clinics in Leicester

The surfaces we prioritise in Leicester

  • Treadmill and bike handles and consoles
  • Parallel bars and balance equipment
  • Therapy balls and foam rollers
  • Check-in counter
  • Door handles
  • Light switches

Our sequence, step by step

  1. Agree which equipment staff wipe between patients and which the cleaning crew handles at end of day.
  2. Clean and disinfect treatment tables and mats with products compatible with vinyl and upholstery.
  3. Wipe down weights, bars and cardio equipment handles and consoles.
  4. Keep gym cloths separate from restroom cloths.
  5. Launder or replace reusable linens per the clinic's process — we do not take clinic linens off site unless contracted.

A starting schedule

  • Treatment tables and shared equipment: between patients by staff, full clean daily.
  • Gym floor: daily.
  • Waiting room: daily.

Clinics with early-morning patients may prefer a pre-opening clean.

What you keep on file

  • Gym and treatment-room checklist
  • Product list with EPA registration numbers and contact times
  • Safety Data Sheets
  • Signed service logs

Survey findings we help Leicester facilities prevent

Real, published regulatory findings — every citation links to its source.

CDC Infection Prevention Checklist for Outpatient Settings, Section II item A; CDC Core Practices 5f

Shared equipment reprocessed in a way the manufacturer never specified. CDC's position is that where no cleaning and disinfection instructions exist, the item is not suitable for multi-patient use.

CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices 5b; CDC Infection Prevention Checklist, Section II item A

High-touch surfaces close to the patient — plinth rails, parallel bars, equipment grips — not cleaned and disinfected on a more frequent schedule than other surfaces.

CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices 5f

Clean and soiled equipment stored together, with no physical separation to prevent cross-contamination.
